title: Court AI: Existing failures set the comparison
desc: Evaluates public information, judicial support and bounded dispute resolution against unmet need while separating multiple reliability risks.

kps.k: The central proposition is to assess court AI against unmet legal need and existing institutional failures, not an idealised human justice system.
kps.d: McCormack, Leonard, Slayton and other contributors frame AI as a possible way to expand access, judicial attention and dispute-resolution capacity. Slayton reports that 70–80% of Los Angeles family-system users represent themselves at some stage; his account of work with Stanford puts eviction defendants’ representation at 14% in the preceding year, against approximately 94% for landlords. These figures establish the stated motivation, not AI’s effectiveness. Slayton argues that inaction carries harms but also warns that rushed deployment, bias or perceived delegation of decisions could undermine public trust even faster.

qs.q: But one of the things I talked to Eli about was, you know, as opposed to what, which is always my first question, like, what are we measuring against?

kps.k: Public information and routine processing offer concrete starting points, but access to a tool does not establish better justice outcomes.
kps.d: Slayton describes Court Help providing eviction-response instructions and form links from official court content, and AI plus robotic processing for 20 document types representing one million annual filings. He reports staff-capacity benefits without accuracy or time-saving measurements. Maricopa chatbots, record-linked Clearbrief tools and proposed multilingual explanations illustrate related approaches. Leonard and Slayton advocate graduated assistance: use AI for initial information and retain people for needs it cannot meet. Reported AI-assisted appeal wins do not establish how much AI contributed to the result.

qs.q: So you can go on Court Help right now and say, “How do I file a response or an answer to an eviction case?” and it gives you step-by-step instructions and links to the forms.

qs.q: Those 20 document types represent 1 million documents filed per year.

kps.k: Judicial decision support attracts both capability claims and objections to outsourcing judgment.
kps.d: Hoffman recommends comparing LLM answers with traditionally reached conclusions to calibrate judgment, interpreting Judge Newsom’s experimentation in that light. McCormack cites Unikowsky’s bounded-brief demonstrations as promising drafting evidence, while acknowledging that useful drafts do not necessarily constitute court-ready work. Klapper markets Learned Hand as case-specific judicial support and reports a summary-judgment task falling from four hours to ten minutes; this is vendor-reported user experience, not a controlled finding about accuracy or fairness. Reported objections to AI-generated opinions and warnings about judges gradually rubber-stamping useful outputs challenge the practical boundary between assistance and substitution.

qs.q: It helps me calibrate my own judgment, which is exactly what we recommended.
qs.a: How AI Is Changing Contract Law with Dave Hoffman — full episode transcript · Academia · 2026

qs.q: You’re correct that we still don’t have a frontier model tool that can basically produce a legal memo that you can just go file in a court—we don’t have that.
qs.a: AI Revolution in 2025? What Lawyers Missed Over the Holidays — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Automated dispute resolution goes beyond judicial assistance, and its proponents generally propose bounded cases, consent and human safeguards.
kps.d: At MAICON 2025, McCormack described a planned AAA AI arbitrator for documents-only construction disputes, supported by an AI-native case-management system, institutional expertise and industry consultation. Elsewhere she explicitly states that AAA’s arbitrator retains a human in the loop. Her 2026 court-resolution forecast concerns experimental, mutually agreed participation in low-stakes, high-volume matters, with possible appeal to a human judge. Nori’s Claimsy proposal similarly offers automated decisions or human-assisted adjudication. These plans and forecasts do not establish completed court pilots, sustainable costs or improved outcomes. McCormack also cautions against assuming that apparently simple disputes lack emotional stakes.

qs.q: And this first use case is just documents-only construction cases.
qs.a: Live from MAICON 2025: Building AAA's First AI Arbitrator — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: **Bridget McCormack:** I should be clear—our generative AI arbitrator does have a human in the loop, because I think that is important.
qs.a: Harvey's Gabe Pereyra on the Future of Legal AI · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Reliability safeguards must distinguish fabricated output, interpretive mistakes, evidentiary authenticity and institutional bias.
kps.d: The discussions distinguish invented authorities from human or AI misreadings of real cases. Some speakers argue that curated sources or task restrictions can avoid fabricated citations; others stress that retrieval-augmented generation does not eliminate hallucinations. Neither prompting models not to hallucinate nor asking them to assess their own competence receives reliability validation here. Deepfake documents and videos create a separate authenticity problem. Participants in Will AI Be Accessible? warn that efficiency-led deployment can bypass human verification and institutional evaluation, invoking Michigan’s automated unemployment-fraud determinations as a cautionary precedent—not a generative-AI performance study. Proposed responses include factual provenance, audit trails, confidentiality controls and meaningful human review.

qs.q: You might have a junior lawyer who doesn’t understand the holding of a case or misses a nuance, but they’re generally not submitting work product to a judge or a partner that has completely made-up case names.
qs.a: Transforming Law with AI: Generative Models, Innovation in Dispute Resolution, and Leadership in Change — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: I thought the RAG process cut down on — well, it does cut down on hallucinations — but the point is, with this technology, it doesn’t eliminate them.
qs.a: The Impact of Generative AI & Driving Innovation within the Court System — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Transparency commands support, but speakers disagree about its legal basis, scope and durability.
kps.d: Leonard reports an argument that appellate review requires distinguishing human-created from AI-created judicial content. McCormack questions that inference, comparing AI with undisclosed clerk contributions and research tools, yet recommends transitional transparency to build confidence. Leonard sees particular relevance where an AI-derived concept could determine a case. McCormack separately interprets Judge McGee’s order as requiring disclosure of AI-built or enhanced evidence. Embedded AI complicates broad non-use affidavits. Pennsylvania’s interim policy, as Leonard describes it, instead permits defined tasks using approved tools under human review, confidentiality and leadership oversight. McCormack predicts that enduring ethical duties may eventually make AI-specific guidance unnecessary; that is not a statement that current requirements have expired.

qs.q: But I’m not sure that it makes sense that disclosing your use of the technology in the course of your decision-making as a trial judge really follows from that.
qs.a: The Future of Generative AI in the Court System & The Importance of Transparency — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: I think, for whatever it’s worth, the dividing line for Judge McGee is if AI was used to build or enhance any kind of evidence that the court or a jury is going to be considering, it has to be disclosed.
qs.a: Private Equity and the Future of Law Firms: Investing in AI — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Institutional capacity and unequal access may determine who benefits more than model availability alone.
kps.d: McCormack and Leonard identify public-budget dependence, technical staffing, training and protected learning time as court constraints. Schlegel argues that funded legal technologists and redesigned case management could produce larger structural gains than isolated drafting tools; his projected timeline reductions remain aspirations. Optimism that public models democratise assistance contrasts with legal-aid participants’ concerns that specialised tools, implementation support and verification capacity remain unaffordable. The claimed quality gap between paid legal tools and public models is not comparatively measured here. Practical proposals include enterprise access, representative judicial experimentation, peer learning and partnerships, while maintaining existing legal-help services.

qs.q: I think there are funding issues, and state courts rely on another branch of government for funding.
qs.a: Can Judges Use AI? Inside the Pennsylvania Supreme Court's Interim Policy — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Judge Scott Schlegel (35:14)  think the biggest crystal ball, if you will, moment will be when courts receive budgets that they can hire a true legal technologist.
qs.a: Bot Overlords, Deepfakes, and the Weight of the Robe — Judge Scott Schlegel on AI in the Courts (The Geek in Review) · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Cheaper legal action could enable valid claims while increasing pressure on courts; the scale and composition of additional filings remain unresolved.
kps.d: McCormack welcomes relief for non-frivolous claims that legal costs and procedural burdens currently make impractical, rather than more litigation indiscriminately. Other discussions raise fears of mass frivolous filings without establishing their likely scale. Slayton reports rising Los Angeles civil filings and attributes the possible contribution of AI-generated pleadings to an NCSC hypothesis. Klapper’s prediction of ten- to twelvefold litigation growth supplies no quantitative basis. The practical implication advanced is to develop court processing and alternative resolution alongside claimant-facing tools, rather than assume cheaper filing will itself deliver timely remedies.

qs.q: Bridget McCormack: I do think the ability for more people with non-frivolous lawsuits to get relief for those wrongs is a good thing.
qs.a: Generative AI and the Courts: Expanding Legal Access or Opening the Floodgates? — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: There's a hypothesis (the National Center for State Courts wrote on this recently, using our data and a couple other states’ data that look very similar to ours) that AI-developed pleadings are driving some of this.
qs.a: AI in LA Courts: David Slayton on Access to Justice — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Public-centred governance links access reform to participation, informed consent and protection of human procedural fairness.
kps.d: McCormack and Leonard favour consumer-focused reconsideration of unauthorized-practice boundaries and task-specific safeguards rather than blanket exclusion. McCormack argues that litigation-driven regulation reflects the disputes resource-rich actors can bring, and urges deliberate policymaking. For court rules, she recommends outreach through legal-services and self-help organisations rather than website notices alone; Austin adds informed consent. The discussions also leave a substantive tension unresolved: respectful human interaction may help parties accept adverse outcomes, while AI-generated explanations might help more people feel heard. Neither prospective fairness gains nor the safety of experimental adjudication is established by the supplied evidence, and proposed legal trials leave client-protection questions unanswered.

qs.q: What I really appreciate about IAALS' approach is that it is trying to move us from a more lawyer-centric approach to a more consumer-facing approach to regulation.
qs.a: GPT-5 and the Future of Legal AI Regulation — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: So if that becomes your regulatory mechanism, you’re getting a skewed sample of disputes.
qs.a: Did AI Just Practice Law? The OpenAI Lawsuit + Legalweek 2026 — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2026

vlens.an: These access-to-justice and civil-society sources accept the proposition that court AI should be judged against unmet legal need and existing institutional failures, while materially developing its practical and governance implications. Their common ground is public-centred: AI may expand affordable assistance or dispute-resolution capacity, but access alone does not establish fair or reliable outcomes, especially where users and institutions lack resources for effective implementation and human verification. Material variation lies in emphasis. Nori advances the affirmative case through Claimsy, a proposed low-cost system for ordinary, low-stakes disputes, with automated adjudication or assistance to a human decision-maker; however, its speed, sustainability and court-relief benefits are projections rather than demonstrated results. The Talk Justice participants are more precautionary, stressing unequal access to specialised tools, insufficient institutional vetting, excessive trust and the risk that efficiency pressures displace human oversight. This is not opposition to court AI: it strengthens the cluster’s comparative framework by specifying safeguards and preserving existing legal-help services. These curated sources illustrate positions within this professional voice and should not be treated as representative of the group as a whole.

qs.q: I worry that people will trust the AI too much, put too much faith in it, and skip those important verification, evaluation, assessment steps.
qs.a: Will AI Be Accessible? · Access to justice · 2023

vlens.an:
This curated set of regulators, judges, court administrators and professional-body contributors accepts the synthesis’s principal proposition and materially develops it. Their common starting point is comparative and public-centred: AI should be assessed against courts already constrained by unrepresented litigants, overloaded dockets, limited staffing and difficult-to-use procedures—not against flawless human justice. They add concrete institutional pathways, including official-information chatbots, routine document processing, record-linked tools, approved low-risk judicial uses, modular procedural review, purpose-built decision support, and narrowly scoped dispute-resolution pilots. Across these proposals, AI is generally framed as a copilot or graduated service layer, with consequential judgment, escalation or appeal retained for humans.

The shared reasons are practical rather than purely technological: expanding public information, increasing judicial attention per case, making valid lower-value claims viable, and releasing staff from routine processing. The sources also converge on safeguards—human verification, confidentiality, audit trails, factual provenance, bounded source material, user consent, selective disclosure and public participation. They repeatedly distinguish demonstrated implementation from claimed outcomes: operational examples and user anecdotes show feasibility or perceived capacity benefits, but do not establish improved accuracy, fairness, access to justice or public confidence.

Material internal variation concerns how far and how fast to proceed. Some contributors concentrate on low-risk information and workflow redesign; others advocate experiments in AI adjudication for documents-only, repetitive or low-stakes matters. Transparency receives broad transitional support, but its legal basis, scope and durability remain disputed: McCormack questions whether appellate review requires disclosure of every judicial AI aid while still favouring openness to build confidence, and other material supports disclosure when AI builds or enhances evidence. Optimism about curated or purpose-built systems is qualified by continuing risks of fabricated authorities, misinterpretation of real cases, sycophancy, overreliance and deepfake evidence. Resource inequality is another tension: public models may broaden access, yet courts, smaller practices and legal-aid organisations may lack the technical staff, training time and verification capacity needed for safe adoption. A small number of supplied excerpts are too tangential to establish a position, particularly those focused mainly on legal education or general AI literacy, but they do not offset the professional voice’s overall constructive extension of the proposition. These sources should not be treated as representative of all regulators, courts or professional bodies, and their number does not indicate prevalence.

qs.q: A system without AI—a system without new technology—has failures and risks as well, and they are significant.
qs.a: AI in LA Courts: David Slayton on Access to Justice — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: So the Pennsylvania Supreme Court (which is the jurisdiction where I'm licensed) now allows the use of approved generative AI tools for certain defined, low-risk tasks, as long as there is human review, strict confidentiality, and leadership oversight.
qs.a: Can Judges Use AI? Inside the Pennsylvania Supreme Court's Interim Policy — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an: The AI-native legal provider source supports the proposition that court AI should be judged against unmet legal demand and existing process failures rather than an idealised human system. It argues that much potentially valuable legal work is currently uneconomic and that AI could compress routine procedural stages while preserving judicial deliberation. Material internal variation tempers this optimism: the account offers predictions rather than measured outcomes, reports only cautious judicial receptiveness rather than endorsement, and raises fabricated citations as an unresolved reliability concern without supplying evidence that Garfield has solved it. Thus, the source supports the proposition’s comparative framing and bounded-use logic, while also reinforcing its warning that access and efficiency claims do not establish reliability or improved justice outcomes.

vlens.an: The selected academia-and-research sources support the proposition that court and legal-aid AI should be assessed against unmet legal need and existing institutional constraints rather than an idealised human system. Their common rationale is that current arrangements already leave courts struggling with overwhelming records and scarce resources, while one-to-one legal services cannot meet consumer demand. Both nevertheless distinguish prospective usefulness from demonstrated effectiveness: the evidence consists primarily of bounded experimentation, reported user needs and approximate or secondhand service figures. They favour augmentation and safeguards rather than unqualified substitution. There is material variation in emphasis: Hoffman focuses on judicial decision support, presenting LLMs as tools for calibrating human judgment and managing records; the legal-aid discussion focuses on scaling consumer-facing assistance and reconsidering unauthorized-practice restrictions, while stressing verification, affordability and informed consent. This is supportive rather than a material extension of the proposition. Because the corpus is curated, these shared views should not be treated as representative of academia and research generally.

vlens.an: Within this curated legal-tech-vendor evidence, Shlomo Klapper supports the proposition that court AI should be judged against courts’ actual capacity constraints rather than an idealised human system. He argues that judges cannot review all filed material and presents purpose-built AI as judicial decision support rather than replacement. His support is conditional on factual verification, provenance, double-checking and demonstrated time savings. The principal internal tension is therefore not whether existing institutional failures justify exploration, but how to preserve judicial judgment and litigants’ need to be heard while proving safety and effectiveness. His claims about capacity and benefits are illustrative or vendor-reported; the supplied evidence provides no measured pilot results on accuracy, fairness or time savings, so it supports the comparison framework more strongly than it establishes successful outcomes.

elens.an: The curated 2023–2024 sources collectively accept the proposition’s comparative baseline: court and legal AI should be judged against unmet legal need, overloaded institutions and imperfect human decision-making, rather than an idealised justice system. They materially develop it through concrete early applications—self-represented-litigant information, multilingual explanations, record-linked analysis, bounded drafting and dispute-resolution tools—and through implementation requirements involving training, public funding, leadership permission, transparency, inclusive rulemaking and informed consent. Material variation lies mainly in emphasis. More optimistic sources foreground expanded capacity, public information and AI-assisted scrutiny of judicial consistency; more cautionary sources stress unequal access to specialised tools, persistent hallucinations, institutional bias and the risk that efficiency pressures displace human verification and oversight. Speakers also differ over the legal basis and future durability of AI-use disclosure, although they generally favour transparency during adoption. Across these sources, assistance is preferred to wholesale replacement, and claimed benefits are usually experiential, anecdotal or prospective rather than measured improvements in accuracy, fairness or justice outcomes. One short AI-literacy excerpt is insufficiently connected to the proposition, but it does not materially alter the period’s overall direction.

qs.q: The civil justice system in America is basically a massive market failure in that 92% of Americans can’t afford help to navigate their civil justice problems.

elens.an: Across this curated 2025 set, the sources accept the proposition that court AI should be assessed against unmet legal need and the failures and capacity constraints of the existing system. They materially extend it by showing adoption moving from general possibility toward operationally specific forms: public-information tools, routine processing at substantial document volume, approved low-risk judicial uses, constrained drafting, consumer self-help, and bounded dispute-resolution initiatives. Common reasons include large representation gaps, burdensome procedure, unserved claims, overloaded court staff and judges, and the prospect of reserving human attention for consequential judgment and procedural fairness. The principal qualification is evidentiary: reported implementations establish activity and sometimes operational scale, but generally do not establish accuracy, fairness, cost savings or improved justice outcomes. Internal variation concerns how far adoption should go. Some sources favour augmentation through triage, preliminary review and human verification; others propose opt-in AI adjudication or an AI arbitrator for restricted case types. Safeguards vary accordingly, including confidentiality controls, closed records, task restrictions, consent, human review and appeal. Other sources shift attention toward consumer regulation, responsible-use education or professional competence, and one source remains too remote from the court-centred comparison to determine a position. Concerns about hallucinations, bias, deepfakes, frivolous filings, unequal access and loss of public trust constrain but do not reverse the period’s overall direction. Because the corpus is curated, this synthesis describes the supplied sources and does not establish how prevalent these views or practices were in 2025.

qs.q: Those 20 document types represent 1 million documents filed per year.
qs.a: AI in LA Courts: David Slayton on Access to Justice — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: So the Pennsylvania Supreme Court (which is the jurisdiction where I'm licensed) now allows the use of approved generative AI tools for certain defined, low-risk tasks, as long as there is human review, strict confidentiality, and leadership oversight.
qs.a: Can Judges Use AI? Inside the Pennsylvania Supreme Court's Interim Policy — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the proposition that court AI should be judged against unmet legal need, constrained judicial capacity and existing institutional failures rather than an idealised human system. They materially develop it through several concrete approaches: purpose-built judicial decision support, bounded low-stakes dispute resolution, human verification and auditable provenance, context-specific disclosure, deliberate public policymaking, and court workflow redesign supported by legal technologists. Common reasons include overwhelming records and caseloads, limited court resources, unaffordable legal help and the prospect of expanding judicial attention or public access. Material variation concerns where AI should operate and how far it should go: some sources favour calibration, research and document management under judge control; Nori entertains automated decisions but also a human-assisted alternative; Schlegel prioritises structural case-management redesign; and McCormack and Leonard emphasise governance and legislative participation. Across the period, claimed benefits are mostly predictions, design proposals, reported demand or vendor/user anecdotes rather than comparative evidence of accuracy, fairness, sustainable cost or improved justice outcomes. The sources also preserve concerns about overreliance, replacement fears, sensitive data, unequal implementation capacity and public trust. This synthesis characterises only the supplied curated sources and does not indicate how prevalent these views are among judges, lawyers or other groups.
